2. Three accused faced trial for the offences punishable under Sections 498A, 302 and 304B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, 'IPC') and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 (for short, 'DP Act').

The trial court acquitted accused Nos.2 and 3 of the offences under Sections 498A, 302 and 304B of IPC and Sections 3 and 4 of DP Act, but convicted accused No.1 for NC:
2023:KHC:40782-DB the offences under Sections 498A and 302 of IPC and Section 4 of DP Act.
Hence, this appeal.
3. The name of the deceased is Suma.
The case of the prosecution is that marriage of the deceased and accused No.1 was performed on 20-3-2014 at Dharmasthala.
During the marriage, the parents of the deceased gave gold ornaments as dowry to accused No.1.
Their relationship was cordial for a couple of days and thereafter, accused No.1 started subjecting the deceased to cruelty in connection with demand for dowry.
On 7-10-2014 at 7.00 a.m., accused No.1 on the instigation of accused Nos.2 and 3 poured kerosene on the deceased and set fire, due to which, she sustained burn injuries.
She was shifted to Victoria hospital for treatment, where PW17-Tahsildar recorded Ex.P15-dying declaration of the deceased on the same day at 3:30 p.m.
On 8-10-2014 at 8.30 a.m., the deceased succumbed to burn injuries.
This led to registration of FIR and investigation.
The prosecution in all examined twenty three witnesses as PW1 to PW23 and relied on twenty-eight documents as per Exs.P1 to P28 and eleven material objects as per MO.1 to MO.11.
For the defence, accused No.1 examined himself on oath as DW1 and got marked Exs.D1 to D13.

The main reasons assigned by the trial court for convicting accused No.1 are that the deceased gave dying declaration as per Ex.P15 before PW17-Tahasildar prior to her death and stated that her marriage was solemnized with accused No.1 on 20-3-2014 at Dharmasthala and during the marriage, sufficient gold ornaments were given in terms of dowry.

After the marriage, they were cordial for couple of days, thereafter, accused No.1 used to quarrel with her saying that if he had married another woman, who possessed a Government job, he would have got sufficient dowry in form of money and she had not brought sufficient dowry from her parental house, thereby subjected her to cruelty.
On the date of the incident, accused No.1 committed murder in connection with demand for dowry, thus, poured kerosene on her and set fire.

The evidence reveals that PWs.1 and 2-mother and father of the deceased respectively,

PWs.6 to 8-inquest mahazar witnesses, PWs.9 to 12-seizure mahazar witnesses, PWs.13 and 14-spot mahazar witnesses, PW15-cousin of the deceased, have turned hostile and have not supported the case of the prosecution.

10. Now, the evidence of PW17-Tahasildar, who recorded the dying declaration in the presence of PW23- Doctor, who certified the mental and physical fitness of the deceased to give statement, is available.
As per the evidence of PWs.17 and 23, the deceased gave statement - 17 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB before them alleging that accused No.1 poured kerosene on her and set fire.
Thus, she sustained burn injuries.

11. As per Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, there can be no dispute that the dying declaration can be the sole basis for conviction, however, such a dying declaration has to be proved to be wholly reliable, voluntary and truthful; the maker thereof must be in a fit medical condition to make it.

12. In the decision rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of NANHAR v. STATE OF HARYANA reported in JT 2010(6) SC 196, it is held that, "dying declaration should be such, which should immensely strike to be genuine and stating true story of its maker.

sentences.text: It should be free from all doubts and on going through it, an impression has to be registered immediately in mind that it is genuine, true and not tainted with doubts.
Further it should not be result of tutoring."
Ex . P15
- dying declaration recorded by PW17- Tahasildar shows that the deceased had suffered severe burn injuries and was admitted to Victoria Hospital and she answered to the questions posed by PW17.
However, a doubt arises as to the manner of recording the dying declaration by PW17.

The contents of Ex.P15 are not in the handwriting of PW17 and it was drafted by CW25, police constable,
and no endorsement is seen stating that the said statement was drafted by CW25 and he was not examined before the trial court.
Hence, PW17 and PW23 simply affixed their signatures to Ex.P15.
It is settled law that, if a dying declaration is truthful, it can lead to conviction.
In the light of the above principle, we have examined the possibility of the dying declaration being a product of tutoring or of imagination of the deceased.
Further, if the declarant was unconscious, she could never have made any declaration.
Such an evidence is to be rejected.

PW17 and PW23 being responsible official witnesses said to have recorded the dying declaration of the deceased, and the trial court ought to have assessed their evidence in strict sense keeping in view Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1972.
In this regard, it is relevant to refer to a judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of JAYAMMA AND ANOTHER v. STATE OF KARNATAKA reported in (2021) 5 SCR 11.

Even prior to her marriage with accused No.1, the deceased attempted to commit suicide and threatened accused No.1 to marry her.

Further, the evidence of PW16-Doctor and DW1 establish that while the deceased caught fire, accused No.1 tried to extinguish it and he also sustained burn injuries on his face and forearms.
Further, PWs.4 and 5, owner of the house (neighbours), where accused No.1 and the deceased were residing have stated that accused No.1 himself shifted the injured to the hospital for treatment.
It shows that the involvement of accused No.1 in the case was very remote.
Further, the parents and cousin of the deceased also have not supported the case of the prosecution.
Merely because of the dying - 21 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB declaration, it cannot be said that the prosecution has proved the guilt against accused No.1.
There is no creditworthy evidence which probabilises that accused No.1 was responsible for the death of the deceased.
15. In the present case, the vital evidence are that of PW17 and PW23 relating to the dying declaration of the deceased at ExP15.

But at a cursory glance of the entire evidence indicates that the theory set up by the prosecution is found to be doubtful and does not inspire confidence in the mind H Hariprakash vs The State Of Karnataka on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199287542/

16. The trial court acquitted accused No.1 of the offences punishable under Sections 304B of IPC and Section 3 of DP Act.
Section 304B of IPC relates to dowry death within seven years from the date of her marriage, but the case ended in acquittal based on the evidence of the prosecution.

When the offences under Section 304B of IPC including offences under Section 3 of DP Act have - 22 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB itself ended in acquittal, i.e., dowry death within seven years from the date of her marriage, naturally it would dilute the strength of the evidence of the prosecution as regards the main offence under Section 302 of IPC.
The motive factor and the intention as regards causing the death of the deceased is the main part to be considered in the instant case.
17. In order to constitute the offence under Section 302 of IPC, it is necessary for the prosecution to establish that there was mens rea and actus rea.
Otherwise, it cannot be construed that there was intention on the part of accused No.1 to eliminate the deceased.
However, the homicidal death of the deceased is not in dispute.
Merely because she had sustained burn injuries, it cannot be said that the offence under Section 302 of IPC has been proved by the prosecution by facilitating worthwhile and acceptable evidence.
Further, the dying declaration does not reveal entire truth and it has to be considered only as a piece of evidence.
Conviction cannot be rested solely on - 23 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB the basis of such doubtful dying declaration.
As per the evidence of PW17, while recording statement of the deceased, her father and mother were present.
If the dying declaration was recorded in presence of the parents of the deceased, the possibility that the deceased was tutored cannot be ruled out.
18. A dying declaration is very important document because it amounts to a statement of the deceased verba dicta.
The dying declaration cannot be treated as wholly trustworthy as it is shrouded with many doubts.
The court must be satisfied that the deceased was in fit state of mind to give statement.
19. In order to prove the case of the prosecution, the medical evidence requires to be corroborated by ocular testimony.
The prosecution has to establish the case by producing positive medical evidence in this regard to prove that the deceased died as a result of burn injuries caused due to the act of accused No.1.

Whereas, there is no corroboration on the part of the prosecution to believe the - 24 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB versions made by the deceased which was recorded as per Ex.P15,
without considering the said fact, the trial court has rendered conviction for offence under Section H Hariprakash vs The State Of Karnataka on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199287542/

sentences.text: On overall assessment of the case of the prosecution, it is found that several witnesses have turned hostile to the case of the prosecution and their contradictory statements have been got marked.

Despite the fact that no cogent and consistent evidence has been facilitated on the part of the prosecution and despite the infirmities and inconsistencies in the statements of witnesses, the trial court has rendered conviction for the offences under Section 498A and 302 of IPC.
The testimonies of the witnesses, even if taken on their face value, fall short of the requirement of proof of the charge beyond all reasonable doubt.

21. From the discussion, it appears that the testimony of PW17 and PW23 appears to be not believable and the evidence of prosecution witnesses does not inspire - 25 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB confidence of the court to prove the guilt of accused No.1 that he committed the murder of the deceased.
If we consider the oral testimony of the prosecution witnesses, it creates suspicion.
Therefore, the benefit of doubt should be extended to accused No.1.
Hence, we are of the opinion that the appeal deserves to be allowed.
Hence, the following O R D E R i.
The appeal is allowed.

ii. The judgment of conviction dated 31-1-2018 and order on sentence dated 6-2-2018 in Sessions Case No.10013/2015 on the file of the IV Additional District and Sessions Judge, Doddaballapura, is set aside.

evaluating the evidence, the trial court came to the conclusion that the prosecution was able to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and held accused No.1 guilty of the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 302 of IPC and Section 4 of DP Act and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for six months with fine of Rs.1,000/- for the offence under Section 498A of IPC, to undergo imprisonment for life with fine of Rs.10,000/- for the offence under Section 302 of IPC and to undergo simple imprisonment for one year with fine of Rs.5,000/- for the offence under Section 4 of DP Act, with further direction to undergo imprisonment for certain term in case of default in paying fine.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
6. Assailing the findings of the trial court, Sri Hashmath Pasha, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant/accused No.1, argues that the trial court has committed an error in convicting the appellant on uncorroborated testimonies of the prosecution witnesses.
Per contra, Sri Vinay Mahadevaiah, learned High Court Government Pleader, submits that though the relatives of the deceased have turned hostile, the relationship, the conduct of accused No.1 and the evidence tendered before the trial court are to be considered.
Their evidence is supported by the evidence of the Doctor and the Tahasildar.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
11. As per Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, there can be no dispute that the dying declaration can be the sole basis for conviction, however, such a dying declaration has to be proved to be wholly reliable, voluntary and truthful; the maker thereof must be in a fit medical condition to make it.
It is settled law that, if a dying declaration is truthful, it can lead to conviction.
PW17 and PW23 being responsible official witnesses said to have recorded the dying declaration of the deceased, and the trial court ought to have assessed their evidence in strict sense keeping in view Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1972.
There is no creditworthy evidence which probabilises that accused No.1 was responsible for the death of the deceased.
15. In the present case, the vital evidence are that of PW17 and PW23 relating to the dying declaration of the deceased at ExP15.
But at a cursory glance of the entire evidence indicates that the theory set up by the prosecution is found to be doubtful and does not inspire confidence in the mind H Hariprakash vs The State Of Karnataka on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199287542/
8
Section 304B of IPC relates to dowry death within seven years from the date of her marriage, but the case ended in acquittal based on the evidence of the prosecution.
When the offences under Section 304B of IPC including offences under Section 3 of DP Act have - 22 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB itself ended in acquittal, i.e., dowry death within seven years from the date of her marriage, naturally it would dilute the strength of the evidence of the prosecution as regards the main offence under Section 302 of IPC.
The motive factor and the intention as regards causing the death of the deceased is the main part to be considered in the instant case.
17. In order to constitute the offence under Section 302 of IPC, it is necessary for the prosecution to establish that there was mens rea and actus rea.
Otherwise, it cannot be construed that there was intention on the part of accused No.1 to eliminate the deceased.
However, the homicidal death of the deceased is not in dispute.
Merely because she had sustained burn injuries, it cannot be said that the offence under Section 302 of IPC has been proved by the prosecution by facilitating worthwhile and acceptable evidence.
Further, the dying declaration does not reveal entire truth and it has to be considered only as a piece of evidence.
Conviction cannot be rested solely on - 23 - NC: 2023:KHC:40782-DB the basis of such doubtful dying declaration.
If the dying declaration was recorded in presence of the parents of the deceased, the possibility that the deceased was tutored cannot be ruled out.
18. A dying declaration is very important document because it amounts to a statement of the deceased verba dicta.
The dying declaration cannot be treated as wholly trustworthy as it is shrouded with many doubts.
The court must be satisfied that the deceased was in fit state of mind to give statement.
19. In order to prove the case of the prosecution, the medical evidence requires to be corroborated by ocular testimony.
The prosecution has to establish the case by producing positive medical evidence in this regard to prove that the deceased died as a result of burn injuries caused due to the act of accused No.1.
On overall assessment of the case of the prosecution, it is found that several witnesses have turned hostile to the case of the prosecution and their contradictory statements have been got marked.
Despite the fact that no cogent and consistent evidence has been facilitated on the part of the prosecution and despite the infirmities and inconsistencies in the statements of witnesses, the trial court has rendered conviction for the offences under Section 498A and 302 of IPC.
The testimonies of the witnesses, even if taken on their face value, fall short of the requirement of proof of the charge beyond all reasonable doubt.
Therefore, the benefit of doubt should be extended to accused No.1.
